newsitem.title: AZERBAIJAN: Chechen leader holds talks with Azeri president.
newsitem.headline: Chechen leader holds talks with Azeri president.

text.p: Chechen leader Aslan Maskhadov met Azeri President Haydar Aliyev on Tuesday in a surprise show of defiance towards Moscow by both men.

Maskhadov temporarily broke what he called a blockade by Moscow on his breakaway republic for the 90-minute meeting with Aliyev in Azerbaijan's capital Baku, the first time he has been received by a foreign head of state.

"The politics of Russia are aimed at blockading us," said Maskhadov, clad in a dark suit and traditional lambswool hat. "We didn't come here to beg, but to discuss questions of mutual benefit," he said before meeting Aliyev.

It was an important propoganda coup for Maskhadov in establishing foreign ties as Russia, which waged an unsuccessful military campaign in 1994-96 to try to stop Chechnya breaking away, insists the Moslem region is still its territory.

The war, which killed tens of thousands, ended with Moscow pulling out its troops and Chechnya agreeing to remain in Russia until 2001. The Chechens say the deal simply allows Moscow to save face pending what they say will be inevitable succcession.

For Aliyev, the veteran Azeri leader who once sat on the ruling Soviet Politburo, hosting the head of the unrecognised state was a daring stunt that risks aggravating the oil-rich republic's already thorny relations with Russia.
It comes just a day before Aliyev sets off to Moscow for his first official state visit to Russia and a meeting with President Boris Yeltsin.
"This meeting was needed to develop friendly ties between our two nations," Aliyev said of the one-on-one session with Maskhadov.

The leaders did not speak to reporters after the meeting. Maskhadov aide Kazbek Khadjiyev said earlier the two men would probably discuss broad political questions and the transit of Azeri oil through a pipeline which crosses Chechen territory.
Russian Prime Minister Victor Chernomyrdin recently signed an agreement with the Chechen leadership on reparing the Chechen section of the route, which runs to the Russian port of Novorossisk.
An $8 billion multinational consortium led by British Petroleum plc plans to use the route for early oil transport from three fields it is developing in the Azeri sector of the Caspian Sea.

Political observers say that Aliyev wanted to show Russia in part that Azerbaijan has trump cards it could play against Moscow if it fails to exert pressure over its traditional ally Armenia, with which Baku has a decade-long territorial dispute.

Azerbaijan has consistently accused Russia of aiding Armenia with weapons and supporting it in the war over the Nagorno-Karabkh enclave which killed more than 35,000 people before a 1994 ceasefire came into effect.
Russian ministers have admitted some of what they call "illegal" arms shipments to Armenia.

No political settlement to the issue has been found despite a recent diplomatic effort by Russia and Western countries to pressure the Armenians to accept a deal giving Karabakh very wide autonomy within Azerbaijan.
"We have made big compromises and are prepared for major concessions to bring an end to this conflict," said Aliyev.
Maskhadov's arrival in a four-car motorcade which travelled more than 400 kilometers from his war-shattered capital of Grozny was given all the trappings of a full state visit.

Streets along the motorcade's route through the heart of the city of three million were closed to traffic two hours before he finally appeared, and elite police troopers armed with automatic weapons lined the way. Maskhadov was expected to return to Grozny on Wednesday morning.
